sections.heading: Start with your lowest month
sections.body: If your income changes every month, build your budget on the smallest amount you earned in the last three months. Anything extra above that becomes savings or debt payments — not spending money.

sections.heading: Essentials first
sections.body: List your essential expenses in order: food, transport to work, rent or accommodation, electricity. Cover these before anything else, and know exactly how much they cost each month.

sections.heading: Give every rand a job
sections.body: When a good month arrives, decide immediately where the extra goes: a portion to savings, a portion to debt, and a small amount for yourself. Deciding in advance stops the money from disappearing.

quiz.q: You earned R8,000, R5,500 and R6,200 over three months. What should your base budget be built on?
quiz.explain: Building on your lowest month means a slow month never puts you into shortfall.

quiz.q: In a good month, the extra money above your base budget should first go to…
options: Savings and debt payments you planned in advance
quiz.explain: Deciding in advance where extra money goes is what turns a good month into a safer future.

sections.heading: Why R1,000 first?
sections.body: Most emergencies — a clinic visit, a tyre, a funeral contribution — cost under R1,000. A small emergency fund stops you from borrowing at high interest the next time something goes wrong.

sections.heading: Save small, save often
sections.body: R50 a week is R2,600 a year. Saving a small amount regularly works better than waiting to save a big amount 'someday'. Even irregular earners can save a fixed share — for example 10% — of whatever comes in.

sections.heading: Keep it separate
sections.body: Keep emergency savings somewhere separate from your everyday spending money so it is not spent by accident. SafeBank's SafePocket helps you track the goal — the money itself stays wherever you choose to keep it.

quiz.q: What is a good first emergency savings target?
options: Whatever is left at the end of the year
quiz.explain: R1,000 covers most day-to-day emergencies and is reachable within a few months.

quiz.q: As an irregular earner, the most reliable way to save is…
options: Saving a fixed percentage of every amount you earn
quiz.explain: A fixed share of every payment — even small ones — builds the habit and the fund.

sections.heading: Interest is the price of borrowing
sections.body: When you borrow R1,000 at 20% interest per year and pay it back over a year, you repay about R1,110 or more depending on fees. The faster you repay, the less interest you pay.

sections.heading: Store accounts add up
sections.body: Store accounts often charge 20%+ interest. A R2,000 account paid with minimum monthly instalments can take years and cost far more than R2,000 in total.

sections.heading: Know your rights
sections.body: Under the National Credit Act, lenders must check that you can afford the loan. If a lender offers credit without checking your income, walk away — and never borrow to pay off another loan.

quiz.q: Borrowing R1,000 at 20% interest means you will repay…
options: More than R1,000 — interest plus possible fees
quiz.explain: Interest and fees are the cost of borrowing; quick repayment keeps them low.

quiz.q: A lender offers you a loan without checking your income or expenses. This is…
options: A warning sign — responsible lenders must check affordability
quiz.explain: The National Credit Act requires affordability checks. Lenders that skip them are dangerous.

sections.heading: What it can look like
sections.body: Financial abuse is when someone controls your access to money — taking your wages or grant, stopping you from working, forcing debt into your name, or threatening you financially. It can happen to anyone, in any kind of relationship.

sections.heading: It is not your fault
sections.body: Economic dependence is often created gradually and deliberately. Wanting financial independence is healthy and normal, and small steps — your own account, your own savings knowledge, knowing what things cost — build towards it.

sections.heading: You can plan quietly
sections.body: SafeBank's Financial Safety section offers private tools: estimating essential living costs, listing trusted people, and learning what support exists. Nothing you plan there is shared or saved on your device.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of financial abuse?
options: A partner and you deciding a budget together
A partner taking your wages and refusing to explain what happened to the money
A family member lending you money with a written agreement
quiz.explain: Controlling or taking your money without agreement is financial control — a form of abuse.

options: Send your plan to the authorities automatically
Keep your planning private, save nothing sensitive on your device, and share nothing without your action
Require you to describe your situation in detail
quiz.explain: The tools are private by design — no disclosures required, nothing stored or shared automatically.
